1.title: Facilitation, Teaching, Mentoring and Coaching
1.text: Welcome to Module 13: Facilitation, Teaching, Mentoring and Coaching. Until now we studied the framework. This module is about the Scrum Master's skills. You will learn when a Scrum Master facilitates, which tools help a group decide, and how to tell four ways of helping apart. Most of the content goes beyond the Guide, but the learning objectives ask for it.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Give three situations where the Scrum Master facilitates. Name three techniques for group decisions, and when to use each. Tell facilitating, teaching, mentoring and coaching apart. Ask the test question: who has the answer? And spot the traps: deciding for the team, and a coach who gives answers.

1.title: Case Check-In: Who Talks, Who Decides
1.text: At RideLoop, a pattern shows in the Retrospectives. Ben talks the most, while Jonas and Sofia rarely speak. Decisions drag on, or they are taken by whoever speaks last and loudest. You are the Scrum Master, and you wonder which stance each moment needs. You also wonder which technique would give everyone a voice. Keep both questions in mind as we go.

1.title: What the Guide Says
1.text: First, what the Guide says. The Scrum Master coaches the team in self-management and cross-functionality. The Scrum Master facilitates stakeholder collaboration when asked or needed. And the Scrum Master leads, trains and coaches the organization as it adopts Scrum. But the Guide does not define the stances. The learning objectives do. In the earlier edition, the Scrum Master facilitated events as requested; today the Scrum Master ensures they happen and are worthwhile.

1.title: Facilitation
1.text: Facilitation means helping a group understand its shared aim and plan how to reach it. The facilitator is active on the process: purpose, structure, time, ground rules, and making sure everyone is heard. And neutral on the content: no side-taking. It is not only for events; it applies anywhere a group needs to work together. A Scrum Master who decides for the team, or argues for one option, is not facilitating. The Guide mentions facilitating once, for stakeholder collaboration, and never defines it, so this definition goes beyond it.

1.title: Where the Scrum Master Facilitates
1.text: The learning objective asks for at least three situations. In the Retrospective, everyone contributes and the team reaches concrete improvements. In Sprint Planning, the Scrum Master helps the team agree one clear Sprint Goal. In refinement, a shared understanding of items. In stakeholder collaboration, as in a Review. In team decisions, like choosing a tool. In agreeing the Definition of Done. And in conflict, where people find their own way forward. The Guide does not list these situations; the list goes beyond it.

1.title: Decision Techniques (1)
1.text: Three techniques for group decisions; they go beyond the Guide. Dot voting: each person places the same number of dots on the options they prefer, which is ideal for choosing several options from a longer list. Roman voting: a thumb up, sideways or down, for a quick check on one proposal. Fist of Five: from a closed fist, which means block, to five fingers, full support, to see how strong the support is. Agree the required level first. Those below it state their concerns, the proposal is adapted, and the group votes again.

1.title: Decision Techniques (2)
1.text: Three more, also beyond the Guide. One-two-four-all: each person thinks alone, then in pairs, then in fours, and then the groups share with everyone. It suits hard topics, or a group far from agreement. Consensus: the group seeks agreement that everyone can live with, with the level set beforehand. It suits decisions everyone must support in practice, but it is slow. Majority vote: more than half wins, for small, low-impact choices, though a minority may disengage.

1.title: Choosing a Technique
1.text: Match the technique to the need. Several items from a list: dot voting. A quick yes or no: Roman voting. How strong is the support: Fist of Five. A hard topic: one-two-four-all, then a vote. Everyone must live with the result: consensus. A small choice: majority vote. For Ben, Jonas and Sofia, one-two-four-all would give the quieter voices a real chance to contribute before the group decides.

1.title: Principles for Any Technique
1.text: A few principles apply to any technique; they come from practice, not the Guide. Agree the method and the threshold before voting. Make sure everyone understands the proposal. Use techniques for the team's own decisions: the Product Owner still orders the Product Backlog, and the Developers still decide how to build. And remember that a decision is only the start. Record it, assign actions, and check later. Techniques never move accountability.

1.title: Four Stances
1.text: Now the four stances. The Guide does not define them, so this slide goes beyond the Guide. One question tells them apart: who has the answer? In teaching and mentoring, the Scrum Master holds the knowledge or the experience, and shares it. In coaching, the coachee holds the answer, and the Scrum Master asks questions. In facilitating, the group holds the answer, and the Scrum Master guides the process. Ask that question in every scenario, and the stance becomes clear.

1.title: Teaching and Mentoring
1.text: Teaching is helping others learn new things, by sharing knowledge or skills. The Scrum Master holds the answer and uses telling and showing, such as explaining the Sprint rules to a new Developer. Mentoring is being a trusted counselor who shares experience. It also means sharing and advising, but it needs real experience in depth, such as sharing how you split large items with a new Product Owner. The Guide mentions coaching but not teaching or mentoring, so these definitions go beyond it.

1.title: Coaching and Facilitating
1.text: Coaching is unlocking potential by helping people learn and find their own answers. The coachee holds the answer, and the Scrum Master asks and draws out. The coach does not necessarily need expertise in the subject. Facilitating is helping a group reach its aim while staying neutral on content. The group holds the answer, and the Scrum Master guides the process, as in a Retrospective or a decision session. The Guide mentions coaching but does not define it, and these definitions go beyond it.

1.title: Which Stance Fits?
1.text: Which stance fits which situation? When the person lacks knowledge of Scrum, teach. When someone wants to learn from a person who has been there, mentor. When a person has the ability but is stuck, or must find their own answer, coach. When a group has to collaborate or decide, facilitate. A Scrum Master moves between these as the situation changes. Coaching is the default for self-management. Choosing between the four stances is practice that goes beyond the Guide.

1.title: Traps: What the Exam Expects
1.text: Here are the traps. Facilitation is neutral, and taking notes or scheduling is not facilitation. Coaching does not give the answer; it asks. Teaching fits a lack of Scrum knowledge. Mentoring needs real experience. Match the technique to the need, and agree the threshold first. And deciding for the team to save time is a typical wrong answer. The best answer helps the team decide, and techniques never move accountability.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Recap. Facilitating is neutral on content and active on process. The decision techniques are dot voting, Roman voting, Fist of Five, one-two-four-all, consensus and majority vote. Teaching and mentoring are where the Scrum Master shares. Coaching is where the coachee answers. The test is: who has the answer? And accountability stays where the Guide puts it. Now test yourself.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. The RideLoop Developers cannot decide between two test tools and the discussion has gone in circles. What should the Scrum Master do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. The Scrum Master facilitates a technique such as Fist of Five with an agreed level of support, so that the Developers decide. Neither the Scrum Master nor the Product Owner chooses for them.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Hana, a new Product Owner on another Lakeshore Transit team, asks you, an experienced Scrum Master, how stakeholder conflicts were handled before. Which stance are you taking by sharing your experience and options? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C, mentoring. Coaching would draw the answer out of Hana, and facilitating would structure a group conversation.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Ben says that arguments with a teammate keep happening and that Ben does not know what to do. You want Ben to find a way forward. Which approach is best? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. Coach Ben: ask what has been tried, what outcome is wanted, and which options exist. Telling Ben, moving Ben, or waiting does not build Ben's own capability.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Which list contains only techniques for group decision making? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A: dot voting, Roman voting, Fist of Five and one-two-four-all. The Daily Scrum, the Sprint Review and the Product Backlog are Scrum events and artifacts, not decision techniques.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Who holds the answer when the Scrum Master is coaching? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D, the coachee. The Scrum Master draws the answer out with questions. In teaching and mentoring the Scrum Master holds the knowledge, and in facilitating the group holds the answer.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: D. Facilitate a technique, and the Developers decide. Question two: C. Sharing experience is mentoring. Question three: B. Coaching draws out the person's own answer. Question four: A. Dot voting, Roman voting, Fist of Five and one-two-four-all. Question five: D. The coachee holds the answer. That completes Module 13. Next, Module 14 covers impediments, technical debt and the organization.
